# Assignment 1. Handwritten digit recognition with K-nearest neighbors

The data file `optdigits.csv` contains information about normalized bitmaps of
handwritten digits, each column representing a pixel in an 8x8 image as an
integer in the range from 0 to 16, with the last column containing the actual
digit. We first loaded the file as a data.frame `digits`.

```{r a1-data}
library(kknn)

# optdigits.csv has no header: 64 pixel columns + last column = digit (0-9)
digits <- read.csv("data/optdigits.csv", header = FALSE)
colnames(digits)[ncol(digits)] <- "digit"
digits$digit <- as.factor(digits$digit)
```

## 1. Data partitioning

```{r a1-split}
n <- dim(digits)[1]
set.seed(12345)
id_train <- sample(1:n, floor(n * 0.5))
train <- digits[id_train, ]

id_tmp <- setdiff(1:n, id_train)
set.seed(12345)
id_valid <- sample(id_tmp, floor(n * 0.25))
valid <- digits[id_valid, ]

id_test <- setdiff(id_tmp, id_valid)
test <- digits[id_test, ]
```

The data.frame `digits` was then split into the following data.frames randomly:

- 50% `train`: 1911 rows
- 25% `valid`: 955 rows
- 25% `test`: 957 rows

For this, we used the code from Lecture 1a ("Holdout in R") and we set a seed
with `set.seed(12345)`.

## 2. 30-nearest neighbor classifier

```{r a1-knn30}
# Fits models
fit_train <- kknn(
  digit ~ .,
  train = train, test = train, k = 30, kernel = "rectangular"
)
fit_test <- kknn(
  digit ~ .,
  train = train, test = test, k = 30, kernel = "rectangular"
)
```

```{r a1-knn30-errors}
# Gets confusion matrices
cm_train <- table(True = train$digit, Predicted = fit_train$fitted.values)
cm_test <- table(True = test$digit, Predicted = fit_test$fitted.values)

# Defines missclass function to calculate classification error
missclass <- function(true, predicted) {
  n <- length(true)
  1 - sum(diag(table(true, predicted))) / n
}

# Defines digit_missclass function to get each digit's classification error
digit_missclass <- function(true, predicted) {
  1 - diag(table(true, predicted)) / rowSums(table(true, predicted))
}

# Shows the error per digit and overall, for training and test data
error_table <- rbind(
  Training = c(
    digit_missclass(train$digit, fit_train$fitted.values),
    All = missclass(train$digit, fit_train$fitted.values)
  ),
  Test = c(
    digit_missclass(test$digit, fit_test$fitted.values),
    All = missclass(test$digit, fit_test$fitted.values)
  )
)
knitr::kable(
  error_table,
  digits = 3, format.args = list(nsmall = 3),
  caption = "Misclassification error per digit and overall ($k = 30$)."
)
```

As expected, we observe the train misclassification error ($0.045$) is smaller
than the test misclassification error ($0.053$). The train error is
slightly smaller as it is calculated on the same data that is used in the
KNN model. This small gap shows little overfitting.

The digit $0$ has the lowest train error at $0.000$ and the third lowest test
error at $0.013$ after the digits $6$ and $7$. The digit $6$ has the lowest
test error at $0.000$ and is tied for the second lowest train error at $0.010$
with the digit $2$. This tells us that these digits are the easiest ones to
recognize in this handwritten set, considering its low resolution.

On the other hand, the digit $4$ has the highest train error at $0.091$ and the
highest test error at $0.138$, followed by $8$ at $0.103$, and $5$ at $0.097$.
The digit $4$ is thus the hardest one to recognize in this dataset.

<!-- Narrower table columns so both confusion matrices fit side by side -->
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}

```{r a1-confusion}
# Shows the confusion matrices side by side
# (rows: true digit, columns: predicted digit).
# The two LaTeX commands centre the tables and leave a 1 cm gap between them
knitr::kables(
  list(
    "\\centering",
    knitr::kable(cm_train),
    "\\hspace{1cm}",
    knitr::kable(cm_test)
  ),
  caption = paste(
    "Confusion matrices for the 30-nearest neighbor classifier:",
    "train (left) and test (right).",
    "Rows are the true digits, columns the predicted digits."
  )
)
```

\setlength{\tabcolsep}{6pt}

Looking at the confusion matrices, the diagonals tell us most samples are
correctly classified as expected. Every other cell outside the main diagonal
contains the samples that were incorrectly classified. On the train data we can
see the most common error was the digit $1$ being misclassified as $2$, followed
closely by $8$ as $1$, which is the most common error on the test data. This
could be due to the dataset's low resolution which does not allow the $8$'s
details in the middle to be displayed clearly. Other common mistakes are
misclassifying the digit $4$ as $7$ or the digit $5$ as $9$. A higher resolution
dataset may decrease the incidence of these errors.

In conclusion, the 30-NN classifier does a good overall job for this dataset,
with a test accuracy of $94.7\%$.


## 3. Easiest and hardest cases of digit "8"

```{r a1-digit8, fig.show="hold", out.width="19%", fig.width=4, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="The two easiest (left) and three hardest (right) cases of digit 8 in the training data. p is the predicted probability of the correct class."}
# Gets the predicted probabilities for the digit 8
idx_8 <- which(train$digit == "8")
prob_8 <- fit_train$prob[idx_8, "8"]

# Gets the 2 samples of 8 with the highest probability and the 3 with the lowest
easiest <- idx_8[order(prob_8, decreasing = TRUE)[1:2]]
hardest <- idx_8[order(prob_8)[1:3]]

# Reshapes one training row into the 8x8 image (pixels are stored row by row)
plot_digit <- function(i, title) {
  img <- matrix(as.numeric(train[i, 1:64]), nrow = 8, byrow = TRUE)
  # heatmap() draws row 1 at the bottom, so reverse the rows to show the
  # digit upright; scale = "none" keeps the raw pixel counts
  heatmap(
    img[8:1, ],
    Colv = NA, Rowv = NA, scale = "none", labRow = NA, labCol = NA,
    main = title, col = grey(seq(1, 0, length.out = 17)),
    # The frame keeps all five images at the same scale in the PDF
    add.expr = box(col = "grey60")
  )
}

for (i in easiest) {
  plot_digit(i, sprintf("Easy: p = %.2f", fit_train$prob[i, "8"]))
}
for (i in hardest) {
  plot_digit(i, sprintf("Hard: p = %.2f", fit_train$prob[i, "8"]))
}
```

Here are the two easiest and the three hardest cases for the digit $8$, that is
the two with the highest predicted probability and the three with the lowest.
With the data resolution, we can clearly see the first two are the digit $8$,
while the last three could be easily mistaken for other digits as the
characteristic round figures from the digit $8$ cannot be observed. These could
be easily mistaken as $1$ or $6$ or some other digit.

In the 64-dimensional space of our features, these cases are not spatially close
to the other samples of the digit $8$, and therefore their predicted probability
of being $8$ is low. Most of their 30 closest neighbors in this space belong to
other classes.


## 4. Misclassification error for $k = 1, \ldots, 30$

```{r a1-misclass}
get_knn_missclass_error <- function(train, valid, k) {
  # Fits models
  fit_train <- kknn(
    digit ~ .,
    train = train, test = train, k = k, kernel = "rectangular"
  )
  fit_valid <- kknn(
    digit ~ .,
    train = train, test = valid, k = k, kernel = "rectangular"
  )

  # Calculates train and validation error rates
  error_train <- missclass(train$digit, fit_train$fitted.values)
  error_valid <- missclass(valid$digit, fit_valid$fitted.values)

  c(error_train = error_train, error_valid = error_valid)
}

# Calculates errors for each value of k from 1 to 30
errors <- sapply(1:30, function(k) get_knn_missclass_error(train, valid, k))
```

```{r a1-misclass-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Training and validation misclassification error for $k = 1, \\ldots, 30$."}
# Optimal k: the first one with the lowest validation error
k_opt <- which.min(errors["error_valid", ])

# Plots the training and validation errors for each k
plot(
  1:30, errors["error_train", ],
  type = "l", col = "blue", ylim = range(errors),
  xlab = "k (number of neighbors)", ylab = "Misclassification error"
)
lines(1:30, errors["error_valid", ], col = "red")

# Dashed line and label at the optimal k
abline(v = k_opt, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
text(
  k_opt, max(errors), paste("optimal k =", k_opt),
  pos = 4, cex = 0.85, col = "grey30"
)
legend(
  "bottomright",
  legend = c("Training", "Validation"),
  col = c("blue", "red"), lty = 1, bty = "n"
)
```

Figure 2 shows a small $k$ returns a more flexible and complex model, while a
large $k$ produces a smoother and simpler model. The misclassification errors
mostly increase as $k$ increases. It is self-evident that using $k=1$ returns an
error of $0$ on the training data as each observation is its own prediction. For
the validation set, the error first decreases and is minimized at $k=3$ and
$k=4$. We are using $k=3$ as it is the first one.

```{r a1-misclass-optimal}
# Sets the optimal value of k
k <- 3

# Fits a new model to get the test error
fit_test <- kknn(
  digit ~ .,
  train = train, test = test, k = k, kernel = "rectangular"
)

# Gets train and valid results
errors <- get_knn_missclass_error(train, valid, k)

# Shows the training, validation and test errors for the optimal k
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Training = errors["error_train"],
    Validation = errors["error_valid"],
    Test = missclass(test$digit, fit_test$fitted.values)
  ),
  digits = 4, format.args = list(nsmall = 4), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste0(
    "Misclassification errors for the optimal $k$ ($k = ", k, "$)."
  )
)
```

For our chosen 3-NN model, the test error is equal to $0.0240$ ($97.6\%$
accuracy), which is very close to the validation error of $0.0251$, so the
validation set was a good guide. Both of these values are considerably larger
than the train error of $0.0115$, which suggests some overfitting. Figure 2
shows that at $k=7$ both error lines are closest to each other, however the
validation error is higher at that point. Overall, the 3-NN model has less than
half the test error of the 30-NN model ($0.053$).


## 5. Cross-entropy for $k = 1, \ldots, 30$

```{r a1-crossentropy}
get_knn_cross_entropy <- function(train, valid, k) {
  fit_valid <- kknn(
    digit ~ .,
    train = train, test = valid, k = k, kernel = "rectangular"
  )
  prob <- fit_valid$prob

  # Indicator matrix I(Y_i = C_m): one row per observation, one column per digit
  Y <- outer(valid$digit, colnames(prob), "==")

  # Cross-entropy as on Lecture 1a, slide 27 (1e-15 avoids log(0))
  -sum(Y * log(prob + 1e-15))
}

cross_entropy <- sapply(
  1:30, function(k) get_knn_cross_entropy(train, valid, k)
)
```

```{r a1-crossentropy-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Validation cross-entropy for $k = 1, \\ldots, 30$."}
# Optimal k: the one with the lowest validation cross-entropy
k_opt_ce <- which.min(cross_entropy)

# Plots the validation cross-entropy for each k (red, as the validation line in
# Figure 2)
plot(
  1:30, cross_entropy,
  type = "l", col = "red",
  xlab = "k (number of neighbors)", ylab = "Validation cross-entropy"
)

# Dashed line and label at the optimal k
abline(v = k_opt_ce, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
text(
  k_opt_ce, max(cross_entropy), paste("optimal k =", k_opt_ce),
  pos = 4, cex = 0.85, col = "grey30"
)
```

Figure 3 shows the validation cross-entropy at different values of $k$. Here, we
observe that the optimal value is $k=6$. We can observe that for small values of
$k$ the cross-entropy is the highest. At $k=1$ every misclassified sample gets
a probability $0$ which adds $-\log(1\times10^{-15})\approx34.5$ to the sum.

Using the cross-entropy may suit a multinomial response better because it is the
minus log-likelihood of the multinomial model. It also uses the predicted
probabilities instead of only using the predicted class. Thus, it rewards the
model's confidence in its correct predictions and penalizes its confident
incorrect predictions as well.


# Assignment 2. Linear regression and ridge regression

```{r a2-data}
# check.names = FALSE keeps the original column names, e.g. "Jitter(%)"
parkinsons <- read.csv("data/parkinsons.csv", check.names = FALSE)

# Keep only the target and the 16 voice features
# (drops subject#, age, sex, test_time, total_UPDRS)
parkinsons <- parkinsons[, c("motor_UPDRS", colnames(parkinsons)[7:22])]
```

## 1. Data partitioning and scaling
```{r a2-partitioning}
n <- dim(parkinsons)[1]
set.seed(12345)
id <- sample(1:n, floor(n*0.6))

train <- parkinsons[id,]
test <- parkinsons[-id,]

# Scale both sets using the same parameters.
train_scaled <- scale(train)

mean_tr <- attr(train_scaled, "scaled:center")
std_tr <- attr(train_scaled, "scaled:scale")

train_scaled <- as.data.frame(train_scaled)
test_scaled <- as.data.frame(scale(test, center=mean_tr, scale=std_tr))
```

## 2. Linear regression

```{r a2-linreg}
# Train, predict, and calculate errors.
# We use ~ . -1 to use all columns for the linear regression and force the intercept to 0
lrm_fit <- lm( motor_UPDRS~. - 1, data=train_scaled)

train_pred <- predict(lrm_fit)
train_mse <- mean( (train_scaled$motor_UPDRS - train_pred)**2 )

test_pred <- predict(lrm_fit, newdata=test_scaled)
test_mse <- mean( (test_scaled$motor_UPDRS - test_pred)**2 )

# Print results
cat("We obtained MSE-Train:", train_mse, "and MSE-Test:", test_mse, "\n")

coef_table <- summary(lrm_fit)$coefficients
significant_vars <- coef_table[coef_table[, 4] < 0.01, 4]
significant_vars <- names(sort(significant_vars))
cat("The most significant variables are, in order:", significant_vars ,"\n")
```

We can see that for our simple linear regression we obtain a reasonable MSE for our train dataset, and greater value for the test. When selecting the most significant variables we are interested in the ones with lowest p-value. Having a low p-value shows that there is statistic evidence that the variable and the target response are strongly related. In our case we selected those variables with p-value less than 0.01 (**), which are: DFA, PPE, HNR, Shimmer.APQ11, Jitter.ABS., NHR, Shimmer.APQ5, and Shimmer.

## 3. Functions 

```{r a2-loglikelihood}
loglikelihood <- function(data, theta, sigma){
    if( sigma <= 0){
        return(-Inf)
    }

    y <- data$motor_UPDRS
    X <- as.matrix(data[, -1])

    n <- nrow(X)

    # loglikelihood for a normal distribution
    loglike <- -n/2 *log(2*pi) - n *log(sigma) - 1/(2*sigma**2) *sum( (y - X%*%theta)**2)

    return( loglike )
}
```

```{r a2-ridge}
ridge <- function(data, theta, sigma, lambda){
    return( -loglikelihood(data, theta, sigma) + lambda*sum(theta**2) )
}
```

```{r a2-ridgeOpt}
ridgeOpt <- function(data, lambda){
    # optim()  --> theta, sigma
    fn <- function(param){
        theta <- param[1:16]
        sigma <- exp(param[17])
        return( ridge(data, theta, sigma, lambda) )
    }

    # Initial values
    par_init <- c((1:16)*0, log(sd(data$motor_UPDRS)))

    result <- optim(par=par_init, fn=fn, method='BFGS')

    return( list(theta= result$par[1:16],
                 sigma=exp(result$par[17])) )
}
```

```{r a2-dof}
DF <- function(data, lambda){
    X <- as.matrix(data[, -1])
    P <- X %*% solve( t(X) %*% X + diag(lambda, ncol(X))) %*% t(X)

    return( sum(diag(P)) )
}
```

# 4. Lambda optimization
```{r a2-lambdas}
lambdas <- c(1, 100, 1000)

for( lam in lambdas){
    params <- ridgeOpt(train_scaled, lam)

    X_train <- as.matrix(train_scaled[, -1])
    pred_train <- X_train %*% params$theta
    mse_train <- mean((train_scaled$motor_UPDRS - pred_train)^2)

    X_test <- as.matrix(test_scaled[, -1])
    pred_test <- X_test %*% params$theta
    mse_test <- mean((test_scaled$motor_UPDRS - pred_test)^2)

    dof <- DF(train_scaled, lam)

    cat("For lambda", lam, "we obtained MSE-Train:", mse_train, "and MSE-Test:", mse_test, "with DOF:", dof,"\n")
}
```

We can see that as lambda grows we obtain a higher MSE for the training dataset, and less degrees of freedom. This behaviour is expected; as we increase the value of our regularization parameter (\lambda) we get simpler models that are a worse fit for our training data. However, we can see that the value of the MSE for the test decreases for \lambda = 100, but then increases again for \lambda = 1000. This Shows that without any regularization, our model is overfitting, and when our parameter is too high we are underfitting. 


# Assignment 3. Logistic regression and basis function expansion

The data file pima-indians-diabetes.csv contains information about the onset of
diabetes within 5 years in Pima Indians given medical details. The dataset
contains in the columns nine variables. The ones which will be considered
in this lab are the second, plasma glucose concentration 2 hours into an oral glucose tolerance test;
the eighth, age (years); and the 
ninth, presence of diabetes (0=no or 1=yes).

```{r a3-data,include=FALSE}
# No header; columns are in the order listed in the lab PDF
pima <- read.csv(
  "data/pima-indians-diabetes.csv",
  header = FALSE,
  col.names = c(
    "pregnant", "glucose", "pressure", "triceps",
    "insulin", "bmi", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"
  )
)
```
## 1. Scatterplot  

The following scatterplot displays plasma glucose concentration against age. Observations are colored according to diabetes status: blue indicates the presence of diabetes, red indicates its absence.

```{r a3-scatter1, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Plasma glucose concentration against age, colored by the true diabetes status."}
# scatterplot of glucose over age, color shows the real diabetes levels
colori <- ifelse(pima$diabetes == 1, "blue", "red")
plot(x = pima$age, y = pima$glucose, col = colori, xlab = "Age", ylab = "Glucose")
legend("bottomright",
  legend = c("Diabetes", "No diabetes"),
  col = c("blue", "red"), pch = 1, bty = "n"
)
```

From the scatterplot, it appears that glucose concentration is more informative for predicting diabetes than age. However, the two classes exhibit substantial overlap, and no clear separation between diabetic and non-diabetic individuals is visible. Consequently, we do not expect diabetes to be easy to classify with a logistic regression model.

## 2. Logistic regression model 

We estimate a logistic regression model using glucose concentration and age as explanatory variables.
The probabilistic equations are: $$P(Y=1 \mid \mathbf{x})=\frac{\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{glucose}+\beta_2\,\text{age})}{1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{glucose}+\beta_2\,\text{age})}$$

and $$P(Y=0 \mid \mathbf{x})=1-\frac{\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{glucose}+\beta_2\,\text{age})}{1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{glucose}+\beta_2\,\text{age})},$$ with the estimated parameters $\beta_0 = -5.912$, $\beta_1 = 0.0356$ and $\beta_2 = 0.0248$. We use a classification threshold of $r = 0.5$. Therefore, an individual is classified as diabetic whenever the predicted probability of diabetes exceeds 0.5.

```{r a3-logistic_model, include=FALSE}
# Logistic model of diabetes over glucose and age obtained with glm function
modello <- glm(diabetes ~ glucose + age,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = pima
)
# Predicted values of the diabetes variable according to the model with
# threshold r = 0.5
predizioni <- predict(modello, type = "response")
predizioni[predizioni <= 0.5] <- 0
predizioni[predizioni > 0.5] <- 1
```


The following scatterplot displays the predicted classifications obtained from the logistic regression model.

```{r a3-scatter2, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Predicted diabetes status of the logistic regression model with threshold $r = 0.5$."}
# scatterplot of glucose over age, color shows the predicted diabetes levels
colori1 <- ifelse(predizioni == 1, "blue", "red")
plot(x = pima$age, y = pima$glucose, col = colori1, xlab = "Age", ylab = "Glucose")
legend("bottomright",
  legend = c("Diabetes", "No diabetes"),
  col = c("blue", "red"), pch = 1, bty = "n"
)
```

The training misclassification error of this model is

```{r a3-misclassification, include=FALSE}
# misclassification error for the logistic model obtained by building the
# confusion matrix
confusion_matrix <- table(
  True = pima$diabetes,
  Predicted = predizioni
)
misclassification_rate <- sum(confusion_matrix - diag(diag(confusion_matrix))) /
  sum(confusion_matrix)
```

$$\text{Misclassification Error}= \frac{\text{Number of Incorrect Predictions}} {\text{Total Number of Observations}} = 0.263$$

The training misclassification error is relatively high. Approximately 26% of the observations are classified incorrectly, which is consistent with the substantial overlap between the two classes observed in the original scatterplot.

## 3. Decision boundary

The decision boundary is obtained by the equation $P(Y=1\mid \mathbf{x}) = P(Y=0 \mid \mathbf{x})$ so we must solve $$P(Y=1\mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \frac{\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{glucose}+\beta_2\,\text{age})}{1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{glucose}+\beta_2\,\text{age})} = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{glucose}+\beta_2\,\text{age} = 0$$

Rearranging for glucose gives $$\text{glucose} =-\frac{(\beta_0+ \beta_2\,\text{age})}{\beta_1} \approx 165.9 - 0.695 \cdot \text{age}$$

The corresponding decision boundary is shown in the following figure.

```{r a3-boundary, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Decision boundary (black line) of the logistic regression model, with the predicted diabetes status for threshold $r = 0.5$."}
# scatterplot, with the classification boundary shown for the basic model
b <- coef(modello)
x1 <- seq(min(pima$age),
  max(pima$age),
  length = 10000
)
boundary <- -(b[1] + b[3] * x1) / b[2]
plot(pima$age, pima$glucose, col = colori1, xlab = "Age", ylab = "Glucose")
legend("bottomright",
  legend = c("Diabetes", "No diabetes"),
  col = c("blue", "red"), pch = 1, bty = "n"
)
lines(x1, boundary,
  lwd = 2,
  col = "black"
)
```

Compared to the true classes, the decision boundary does not appear to capture the underlying relationship between the variables particularly well, as more than half of the diabetic patients lie below the line. A simple linear boundary may be too restrictive for this dataset where the main problem is the huge overlap between the classes.

## 4. Different thresholds
In this section, we investigate how the classification results change when different probability thresholds are used.

First, we reduce the classification threshold to 0.2. Consequently, observations with a predicted probability greater than 0.2 are classified as diabetic. This is the corresponding scatterplot:

```{r a3-scatter_r02, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Predicted diabetes status of the logistic regression model with threshold $r = 0.2$."}
# scatterplot of glucose over age, color shows the predicted diabetes levels
# obtained using the threshold r = 0.2
predizioni_r02 <- predict(modello, type = "response")
predizioni_r02[predizioni_r02 <= 0.2] <- 0
predizioni_r02[predizioni_r02 > 0.2] <- 1
colori_r02 <- ifelse(predizioni_r02 == 1, "blue", "red")
plot(x = pima$age, y = pima$glucose, col = colori_r02, xlab = "Age", ylab = "Glucose")
legend("bottomright",
  legend = c("Diabetes", "No diabetes"),
  col = c("blue", "red"), pch = 1, bty = "n"
)
```

We can see that the number of predicted cases of diabetes increases considerably. Conversely, increasing the threshold to 0.8 leads to a much smaller number of positive classifications, as shown in the following plot.

```{r a3-scatter_r08, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Predicted diabetes status of the logistic regression model with threshold $r = 0.8$."}
# scatterplot of glucose over age, color shows the predicted diabetes levels
# obtained using the threshold r = 0.8
predizioni_r08 <- predict(modello, type = "response")
predizioni_r08[predizioni_r08 <= 0.8] <- 0
predizioni_r08[predizioni_r08 > 0.8] <- 1
colori_r08 <- ifelse(predizioni_r08 == 1, "blue", "red")
plot(x = pima$age, y = pima$glucose, col = colori_r08, xlab = "Age", ylab = "Glucose")
legend("bottomright",
  legend = c("Diabetes", "No diabetes"),
  col = c("blue", "red"), pch = 1, bty = "n"
)
```

## 5. Function expansion
We now perform a basis function expansion by introducing five additional polynomial covariates: $z_1 = \text{glucose}^4$, $z_2 = \text{glucose}^3\,\text{age}$, $z_3 = \text{glucose}^2\,\text{age}^2$, $z_4 = \text{glucose}\,\text{age}^3$, $z_5 = \text{age}^4$. The probabilities in this new model will be $$P(Y=1 \mid \mathbf{x})=\frac{\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{glucose}+\beta_2\,\text{age}+\beta_3 z_1 + \beta_4 z_2 + \beta_5 z_3 + \beta_6 z_4 + \beta_7 z_5 )}{1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{glucose}+\beta_2\,\text{age}+\beta_3 z_1 + \beta_4 z_2 + \beta_5 z_3 + \beta_6 z_4 + \beta_7 z_5 )}$$
and $$P(Y=0 \mid \mathbf{x})=1 -\frac{\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{glucose}+\beta_2\,\text{age}+\beta_3 z_1 + \beta_4 z_2 + \beta_5 z_3 + \beta_6 z_4 + \beta_7 z_5 )}{1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{glucose}+\beta_2\,\text{age}+\beta_3 z_1 + \beta_4 z_2 + \beta_5 z_3 + \beta_6 z_4 + \beta_7 z_5 )}$$

The predicted classifications obtained from the expanded model are shown in the following scatterplot.

```{r a3-scatter_expanded, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Predicted diabetes status of the logistic regression model with the basis function expansion (threshold $r = 0.5$)."}
# creation of the variables for the expanded model
pima$Z1 <- pima$glucose^4
pima$Z2 <- pima$glucose^3 * pima$age
pima$Z3 <- pima$glucose^2 * pima$age^2
pima$Z4 <- pima$glucose * pima$age^3
pima$Z5 <- pima$age^4
# logistic regression of diabetes over glucose, age and the five new variables
modello_expanded <- glm(diabetes ~ glucose + age + Z1 + Z2 + Z3 + Z4 + Z5,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = pima
)
pred_expanded <- predict(modello_expanded,
  type = "response"
)
pred_expanded[pred_expanded <= 0.5] <- 0
pred_expanded[pred_expanded > 0.5] <- 1
# scatterplot of glucose over age, color shows the predicted diabetes levels
# according to the expanded model
colori_exp <- ifelse(pred_expanded == 1, "blue", "red")
plot(x = pima$age, y = pima$glucose, col = colori_exp, xlab = "Age", ylab = "Glucose")
legend("bottomright",
  legend = c("Diabetes", "No diabetes"),
  col = c("blue", "red"), pch = 1, bty = "n"
)
```

```{r a3-misclassification_expanded, include=FALSE}
# Training misclassification error of the expanded model
misclass_rate_expanded <- mean(pred_expanded != pima$diabetes)
```

Unlike the original logistic regression model, the decision boundary is not linear and instead takes a curved shape. We can now obtain the misclassification error for this model: $$\text{Misclassification Error}= \frac{\text{Number of Incorrect Predictions}} {\text{Total Number of Observations}} = 0.245$$

The misclassification error is slightly lower than that of the original logistic regression model. This suggests that the basis function expansion captures additional nonlinear structure in the data and provides a modest improvement in predictive performance on the training set.


# Assignment 4. Theory

## Why can it be important to consider various probability thresholds in classification problems?
When we are dealing with a dataset to train a classification model, and
the resulting model is calibrated, a threshold of $r=0.5$ minimizes the
misclassification error. However, at
times, it is more beneficial to optimize different classification metrics
(precision, recall, etc.), and it could be more important to correctly identify
one class over others. The book provides this example: in medical diagnosis, it
can be worse to incorrectly predict a sick patient is healthy than to predict a
healthy patient is sick, and this problem can be imbalanced due to the rare
diseases' low prevalence. The threshold controls the trade-off between false
positives and false negatives in a confusion matrix (pp. 54, 89-92).

## What ways of collecting correct values of the target variable for supervised learning problems are mentioned in the book?
- Recording the target values together with the inputs (p. 16). e.g.: Soccer
results, historical apartment prices (p. 6).

- Labels can be created by a domain expert based on the input data (p. 16). 
e.g.: a cardiologist needs to look at each ECG signal and determine the heart
condition that is present.

- Labels can be created automatically (p. 6). The supervision is not done by a
human domain expert.

## How can one express the cost function of linear regression in matrix form?
In a linear regression model, the predicted values are obtained by the relation $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\theta}$. We use the squared error loss, whose formula is $L(\hat y(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}), y) =(\hat y(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}) - y)^2$, to estimate $\boldsymbol{\theta}$. The cost function $J(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ in matrix notation can be written, according to the book, at page 45, as: $J(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{n}\|\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{y}\|_2^2$.
